title: File:Risotto of leek, mushroom, pea, spinach - Relish Food Store AUD14 (4139673555).jpg
description: I was hungry, so I went for a hearty risotto. It was very tasty, and obviously made with a good stock. I would have been happy to have just a leek and mushroom risotto. Julia thought that the peas seemed to detract from the rich, silkiness of the rice, and I agreed. In that old-skool way, the waitress asked if I'd like cracked pepper on it, even before I had a chance to taste it :) Just as well I declined. The seasoning was fine just as it was. --- Relish Food Store (03) 9578 9058 256 McKinnon Rd McKinnon VIC 3204 Reviews: - Relish Food Store - www.miettas.com.au/ The Age Cheap Eats 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009; The Age Good Food Guide 2005, 2006 - Postcodes: 3204 Ormond - by Carolyn Holbrook, Epicure, The Age, November 28, 2006 A champion of consistently high-quality food that keeps everyone from fussy five-year-olds and food-trendy mums to keep-it-plain-and-simple grandmas happy. Love the salmon, dill and potato cakes, egg and bacon pie and baked lemon cheesecake.

title: File:Vermicelli alle vongole lupino.jpg
description: E' tradizione  che in occasione della cena della Vigilia di Natale, si prepari  un menù  di pesce, dove la prima portata sarebbe costituita dagli spaghetti alle vongole. Sembra che questa usanza abbia origini antiche e che sia  tramandata  dal  primo piatto di spaghetti alle vongole che sarebbe stato servito alla vigilia di Natale del 1762 alla corte di Ferdinando IV di Borbone, re del Regno di Napoli. Inoltre il libro 'Cucina teorico-pratica' di Ippolito Cavalcanti,  pubblicato nel 1837 parla dei vermicelli all’aglio con le vongole

description:
Orecchiette con cime di rapa  AUD22 
Hand shaped Puglia style wholemeal pasta, pigs cheek, "cime di rapa" potato, chilli, pecorino  
  I loved the bite of the wholemeal orecchiette. It was a nice foil to the rich olive oil and crisp wafers of cured pigs cheek. The cured pigs cheek tasted a bit like prosciutto, but the texture seemed finer and the flavour intensified by the baking or frying. In between the chewy pasta were tender kipfler potatoes and the contrasting bite of the cime di rapa.

title: File:Gnocchi al pesto - homemade.jpg
description:
A matter of legacy: Pesto sauce.
 One of the sweetest memories of my childhood, is the moment when I used to help my mother preparing Pesto sauce.
We left Genoa and we emigrated to a small village on the Swiss border, when I was just a little girl.
Preparing Pesto, for my mother and my family was something like going back home.
That’s why it was so important for my mother to make it only when, coming back after visiting my grandparents and uncles based in Genoa, we could bring home, like a trophy, the original Genoese basil: Prà basil.
This basil has a particular sensory quality, that makes Pesto a very special sauce: tasty, genuine and, above all, healthy.
Its essential oils make it magic and you can easily recognize it from the scent, the color and the shape of the leaves. Remember, if you want to live this mystic experience: small, light green leaves in the shape of a teaspoon!
So even now, when I’m going to make homemade Pesto, I blindly follow my mother’s law: “Don’t make Pesto, if you can get Prà basil!”.
Furthermore, basil is not the only issue, when one talk about traditional Pesto sauce.
This sauce is a matter of legacy. Even if the modern recipe is not so ancient, it dates back to the beginning of the 20th century, it preserves the echoes of ancient recipes and know-hows coming especially from the Romans and from the Arabs.
It is the case for garlic, a disinfectant, and for coarse salt, known for its preservative properties. It is the case of pine nuts, strictly coming from Pisa, and of the two traditional cheese, Parmigiano Reggiano and Pecorino Sardo. But, it’s also a matter of the know-how and backstory behind marble mortar and pestle, the traditional tools used since the origin of this and other Ligurian sauces.
In my opinion there is nothing so impressive and evocative as to get intensely inside the traditional cuisine of a place, in order to deeply grasp the meaning of its history and its evolutions.
But now let me bring you inside the family recipe and some tips that my mother passed on to me.
Seven are the ingredients and seven are the steps and the tips that I’m going to give you, let’s start!
1)	First step and first ingredient: garlic, possibly organic and Italian (top choice: Aglio from Vessalico). Peel it and remove the germ from the garlic clove and start to beat it inside the mortar;
2)	Add Pisa pine nuts (25/30 gr.) and keep beating them into a pulp.
3)	Put in 1 teaspoon of coarse salt and mix it.
4)	And now comes the moment of “his majesty” - basil: the leaves of one small bunch for each guest; this is one of the most crucial moments. As I told you before, basil boats very delicate and healthy essential oils and it’s extremely important to preserve them. So if you use the mortar and the pestle the movement should be precise and quick. If you are using a food processor, it’s vital, first of all,  to keep the  blender jar in the freezer for about an hour. It’s mandatory not to over heat the basil. So please be careful.
5)	Now you can add Parmigiano Reggiano (about 65/70 gr of 18/24 months aged cheese) freshly grated.
6)	And then you can add Pecorino Sardo (about 30/35 gr of 10 months cheese) freshly grated too.
7)	At the and of this process of melting and beating, another key moment: EVO, best if Ligurian. The quantity depends on the consistence we want to obtain that could be a little bit different according to the kind of pasta that you are going to dress. But it also crucial to add the oil scantily, without stopping to mix the sauce	
And that’s it, folks! Very soon Pesto sauce will be ready and your guests will be delighted and in love with it. 
And remember… it’s a family secret! ;-)
Ps. 
 
leave a comment below, if you would like more information on the history of the pesto or on the recipes related to it
author: Fuerteadventours

title: File:02026 0377 Between chapters.jpg
description: The closest kin to our beloved Polish bean stew is actually Cassoulet, hailing from Southern France (Languedoc, mind you, NOT Brittany). It’s a slow-cooked, indulgent affair of white beans, meats—often duck or goose—and posh local sausages. The Poles likely hijacked this hearty, one-pot blueprint, stripping it down to local essentials: pork and tomatoes. In the world of classic French cuisine, the term à la bretonne refers to dishes served with white beans (most notably the prized Coco de Paimpol variety), which is the pride of Brittany. So, our 'Brittany-style' beans are basically a fancy French name for a brilliantly simplified Polish comfort food.
author: Marsilar

title: File:Bouilli quebecois.jpg
description:
Si la tradition du bouilli demeure bien présente dans les familles dès la fin de l'été en région, il existe autant de recettes pour ce plat que pour les tourtières du Lac-Saint-Jean. Le chou, les carottes, les pommes de terre, les navets, les oignons et les petites fèves sont la base d'un bon bouilli maison. Bien sûr, l'assaisonnement avec les épices ajoute un plus et devient le secret maison de cette recette.
Le bouilli porte ailleurs l'appellation de «pot-au-feu». De l'épaule, de la macreuse, du jarret ou la palette du boeuf constituent la viande nécessaire au bouilli, certes, mais il faut aussi beaucoup de lard de porc, de porc salé et aussi des bas morceaux avec os.

title: File:Chocos y mariscos frescos.jpg
discoveryCategory: Dish-first search: Pulpo a la Gallega
description:
El choco es un molusco cefalópodo de cuerpo ovalado y ancho bordeado por una aleta con la que se desplaza nadando por el fondo marino, posee una concha calcárea en su interior de la que copia uno de sus nombres, la jibia. El choco o sepia presenta 10 brazos alrededor de su boca, de los cuales dos son más grandes y emplea para capturar sus presas, alimentándose normalmente de pequeños peces, crustáceos y moluscos que paraliza con su saliva y trocea con el pico de su mandíbula.
 El choco siempre nos fascina por su capacidad de mimetización, con una coloración cambiante gracias a la acción de sus cromatóforos que alternará las bandas claras y oscuras en tonalidades que irán desde el gris al marrón o al violeta.
  El choco es una especie dioica, sexos separados, que se reproduce en los meses de marzo y abril, en plena primavera. El macho corteja a su amada luciendo unos llamativos colores y realizando un baile nupcial que culminará en un abrazo tras el que se produce la fecundación de los huevos que serán depositados, uno a uno, entre algas u objetos del fondo. El macho acompañará en todo momento a la hembra, que morirá una vez finalizado el desove, por lo que la sepia solo se reproduce una vez a lo largo de su vida. La esperanza de vida del choco es de entre 18 meses a 2 años.
  El choco habita en fondos arenosos o fangosos poblados por algas, una especie que podemos encontrar en las costas atlánticas y el Mediterráneo, siendo los ejemplares obtenidos en aguas de la costa gallega de una calidad superior gracias al hábitat donde se desarrollan estos moluscos cefalópodos, aguas de excelente calidad con gran diversidad y riqueza de especies que servirán de alimento a estos animales, lo que ve reflejado en sus cualidades organolépticas.
  Las capturas de choco  se realizan de modo artesanal mediante artes de pesca como las nasas para choco, los trasmallos, los miños, el arrastre como el boliche o el chinchorro y las poteiras. Artes de pesca respetuosas con el producto que lo convierte en una especie muy demandada por la calidad de su carne, siendo la mayor parte comercializadas en fresco.
Diferencia entre choco y calamar
 
El choco y el calamar no son el mismo animal, su nexo de unión es la clase a la que ambos pertenecen, cephalopoda, ya que tanto el calamar como el choco son moluscos cefalópodos y como tales presentarán una serie de características que los asemeja, aunque sus diferencias son evidentes si colocamos ambos ejemplares juntos
author: PEPE GADEIRAS

description:
The Filipino version of Chop Suey is a celebration of fresh, locally available produce, creating a vibrant and satisfying dish.
In a traditional Filipino Chop Suey, an assortment of vegetables including carrots, bell peppers, snow peas, baby corn, and cabbage is skillfully sliced and stir-fried to maintain their crisp texture. Complementing the vegetables, meat options like chicken, pork, or shrimp are often added, providing a savory and protein-rich element.

title: File:Kung Pao Chicken - Jadeland Restaurant, Ottawa (6453176819).jpg
description: Gong Bao Ji Ding at the Jadeland Restaurant, Ottawa - August 19, 2011 Appeared on the menu as 'Kung Po Chicken' in English and 宫保鸡丁 in Chinese characters. A very poor effort for what is supposed to be a Sichuan restaurant. The chicken was sliced instead of cut into cubes despite saying '丁 ' on the menu. There were no chilli pieces and no scorched chilli taste. Cashews were used instead of peanuts. There was very little chicken and lots of vegetables used for bulk. These included diced carrot and bamboo shoot, peas, celery, baby corncob chunks and big pieces of green pepper. The chilli consisted only of very fine flecks in a mediocre sauce which was nondescript and would have been at home in a canned chop suey. www.jadeland.com/
author: John Thompson  from Iqaluit

title: File:Hemerocallis lilioasphodelus (1).jpg
description:
Lemon Day-lily Lemon Lily, Yellow Day-lily. Found across China, in Europe in N.E. Italy and Slovenia.
  The flowers of some daylillies, including  Hemerocallis lilioasphodelus  are edible and are used in Chinese cuisine. They are sold (fresh or dried) in Asian markets as gum jum or golden needles (金针 in Chinese; pinyin: jīnzhēn) or yellow flower vegetables (黃花菜 in Chinese; pinyin: huánghuācài). They are used in hot and sour soup, daylily soup (金針花湯), Buddha's delight, and moo shu pork.

title: File:Bean Jelly, Gong Bao Chicken Rice, Cumiin Lamb Ribs - Sichuan House (4304028095).jpg
discoveryCategory: Dish-first search: Gong Bao Ji Ding
description: The 锦绣凉粉 combination bean jelly was slippery and smooth, and it had a wonderful sesame and peanut sauce flavoured with liberal amounts of garlic and 花椒 Sichuan pepper! On the side was a small mound of pork sautéed until the meat was dry and the Sichuan pepper-laced sauce syrupy and caramelised. The 宫宝鸡丁饭 Kong Pao Chicken was quite good too. Spicy, sweet and sour. Just like I remember when Chee Yeen had it! The fragrance of the 孜然 cumin, 花椒 Sichuan pepper and garlic was amazing when this arrived! The lamb ribs were very tender. Some of the ribs even had crunchy soft bone cartilage from the ribs! I think I would have preferred pork ribs and less cumin. The lamb ribs are greasy to begin with and the deep frying didn't help! 川府酒家 Sichuan House (previously 天府川菜馆 Dainty Sichuan) (03) 9650 8589 22-26 Corrs La Melbourne VIC 3000

title: File:Ju Xiang Yuan Restaurant, Ottawa - Gong Bao Ji Ding (6453794127).jpg
discoveryCategory: Dish-first search: Gong Bao Ji Ding
description:
Ju Xiang Yuan Restaurant, Ottawa - Gong Bao Ji Ding
 
Best I have had in a restaurant as of yet. The picture in the menu made it look a little insipid but the real thing was pleasantly golden red. There were lots of white chicken cubes and peanuts with short sections of finger size red chilies. The non standard item was cucumber which gave it a nice colour balance but it didn't add to the dish flavour-wise. It was, however, only added in a fairly small amount and not obviously included just to give bulk to the plate. The sauce leaned to being quite sweet but with a good heat level and the proper scorched chilli taste that is essential to this dish. Overall, the heat was enough to make it interesting but not overwhelming. This is way I would make it. Rated at 5/5
author: John Thompson  from Iqaluit

title: File:Three Kings Restaurant, Ottawa - Gong Bao Ji Ding (6454761105).jpg
discoveryCategory: Dish-first search: Gong Bao Ji Ding
description:
Three Kings Restaurant, Ottawa - Gong Bao Ji Ding
 
This appeared on the menu as Kung Paw Chicken (宫保鸡丁). The chicken was generally, but not exclusively, cut in cubes. and there were cashews instead of peanuts. There were no chilli pieces in dish but there were some flecks of dried chilli in the sauce.  The dish was quite spicy hot but had no scorched chilli flavour and there was no sweetness to the sauce at all. Lots of veggies were included for bulk . There were chunks of celery, carrot, and onion, baby corn cob pieces and canned water chestnut slices. There is also green and red pepper added along with sliced button mushrooms. The mushrooms actually complemented the dish very nicely.  Not bad but not great. Rating: 3 out of 5.
author: John Thompson  from Iqaluit

title: File:Roasted Salmon Skin sushi roll, Soft Shell Crab sushi roll, Salmon and Avocado sushi roll, Miso Soup - Kenzan GPO (2673449759).jpg
description: Roasted Salmon Skin sushi roll AUD3, Salmon and Avocado sushi roll AUD3, Soft Shell Crab sushi roll AUD3.90, Miso Soup AUD3 - Kenzan GPO --- At a quarter past 12 on Friday, Kenzan is already nearly fully packed. I order my Winter Special of Tonkotsu Ramen and grab a table to wait for Julia. Julia arrives soon after, and orders a few sushi rolls and miso soup. We've always loved the sushi rolls at Kenzan, especially since the nori seaweed sheets are packed separately, ensuring a fresh crunchy sushi when you put it all together. Julia got our favourite soft shell crab. yum! We also try a roasted salmon skin sushi which was good too. Eventually, my Tonkotsu Ramen arrives and it looks amd smells great! The soup is not as milky nor as garlicky as some, but it is flavourful pork bone soup. Very good, better than the Chasu Ramen, which was good. Kenzan At GPO Shop 28g / 350 Bourke St Melbourne VIC 3000 (03) 9663 7767 Photos: - Queue - Roasted Salmon Skin sushi roll, Soft Shell Crab sushi roll, Salmon and Avocado sushi roll, Miso Soup - Tokotsu Ramen - Chasu Ramen

title: File:Gyu Don - Sushiko (2649809662).jpg
description: Gyu Don - Sushiko AUD10 --- A new Japanese restaurant is always worth a try. We didn't have too high hopes for this place because we could tell that it wasn't owned/run by Japanese. We were right. It was a young guy with ties to HK, but born here. He suggested we try the agedashi tofu, so we did. It wasn't bad, but I got a piece of tofu that had a goopy batter, which should have been light and spongey. The other pieces were fine though. He also suggested a sukiyaki beef main, but we opted for the gyu don, beef with egg sauce on rice. This was quite nice, but there was something typically Chinese about it. We noticed the ramen with pork bone soup, so we ordered it, ever hopeful that we might get a decent Kyushu-style tonkotsu milky bone soup. The soup was good, for a Chinese pork bone soup. Somehow, it was missing something. Being a kaiten sushi place, wee had to try some sushi. The sushi doing the rounds on the conveyor belt were predictably semi-dried out, verging on crusty! Encouraged by the friendly and enthusiastic owner, we decided to order a tuna and eel to see if that was any better. Nope. One piece of tuna was still on the icy side, and both plates had stone cold, hard rice that wasn't flavoured enough. So much for a second chance. Also on offer was a shabu shabu Japanese hotpot, for AUD25 a set, to serve 2, including a plate of sushi and a dessert. Would we go back? Perhaps for the ramen, but definitely not the sushi. title: File:2013 Tam Lao.jpg
description: A plate of   som tam Lao   (Thai script: ส้มตําลาว). The name is sometimes shortened to just   tam Lao  . This version of green papaya salad will contain fermented fish ( pla ra  or  padaek ), chillies, pickled rice paddy crab, lime, yardlong beans, tomato, sugar, Thai aubergine, and shredded green papaya. This particular version also contains tamarind juice for added "smoothness" and  makok  (the fruit of the  Spondias mombin  of which the large seed is easily recognisable on the right hand side of the dish).

title: File:DSCF0811 A vibrant plate of Thai green papaya salad with cherry tomatoes lime shellfish and squid in a tangy sauce.jpg
description: This photo shows a delicious-looking Thai papaya salad (Som Tam) served on a white plate. The dish features julienned green papaya strands mixed with fresh vegetables including sliced cherry tomatoes and what appears to be small squid or seafood pieces. You can also see some small clam or cockle shells mixed throughout the salad. The dish has a glistening appearance suggesting a tangy dressing, likely made with fish sauce, lime juice, chili, and palm sugar - ingredients typically used in this popular Thai dish. The background is softly blurred, indicating it was photographed in what seems to be a restaurant setting. Som Tam is known for its perfect balance of sweet, sour, salty, and spicy flavors, and is a staple in Thai cuisine, particularly popular in the northeastern (Isaan) region of Thailand.

title: File:Kalyani Biriyani.jpg
description:
Kalyani biryani
 Kalyani biryani is a typical biryani from Hyderabad.[20] Also known as the 'poor man's Hyderabadi biryani, the Kalyani biryani is always made from small cubes of buffalo meat. It doesn't have the same level of expensive ingredients and richness as the more famous Hyderabadi biryani, but at the same time, is quite tasty.
  The meat is flavoured with ginger, garlic, turmeric, red chili, cumin, coriander powder, lots of onion and tomato. It is first cooked as a thick curry and then cooked along with rice. Then given dum (the Indian method of steaming in a covered pot).
  The Kalyani biryani is supposed to have originated in the Bidar during the reign of the Kalyani Nawabs, who migrated to Hyderabad after one of the nawabs, Ghazanfur Jang married into the Asaf Jahi family. The Kalyani biryani was served by the Kalyani nawabs to all of their subjects who came from Bidar to Hyderabad and stayed or visited their devdi or noble mansion.
 
This was the practice for many decades. But after Operation polo in which the Indian army took over Hyderabad State, the state of the nobles went into decline. Some of their illustrious cooks set up their own stalls and introduced the Kalyani biryani. to the local populace of Hyderabad.
author: Clickzvkd

description: This hearty banquet plate brings together aromatic spiced rice, fluffy steamed vattayappam, rich slow-cooked meat gravy, fried chicken, cooling yogurt raita, tangy mango/lime pickle, and creamy semiya payasam. Widely served at weddings, festive occasions, and communal gatherings across Kerala and southern India, meals like this reflect India's rich culinary traditions and love for generous, flavorful hospitality.

title: File:Amma ka Rogan Josh.jpg
description:
This is the picture from last Eid when there is a tradition in my family to indulge upon recipes from the Muslim Kitchens..since we belong to a Non-Muslim family but we believe to celebrate such and such cross cultural cuisines beyond the boundaries of only one community. And yes if we talk about the title of this picture,"Amma ka Rogan Josh", I chose this title because my mother has inherited this recipe from her mother, and we are trying to preserve this recipe as a heritage to my Indian culture of multiculturalism and appreciation of old age recipes.
 Rogan (روغن) means "oil" in Persian, while Josh (جوش) means "heat, hot, boiling, or passionate". Also Rogan implies to the red colored curry, the extensive use of Kashmiri red chillies being the reason.
  Rogan Josh is a curry based dish comprising lamb or mutton pieces simmering in the flavored stew till the Rogan(fats/oil) gets separate from the meat. Onions and yogurt are the original thickening agent to the gravy but tomatoes are additional incorporation in the recent centuries. ( Source- The Great Curries of India, Panjabi, Camelia,1995)
  Rogan josh is a signature dish of Kashmiri cuisine and is one of the main #dishes of the Kashmiri multicourse meal (the wazwan). The dish was brought to Kashmir by the Mughals, the date is quite unclear, whose cuisine was, in turn, influenced by Persian cuisine. The unrelenting summer heat of the Indian plains took the Mughals frequently to kashmir , which has a cooler climate because of its elevation and latitude.
 
So,yes this is one of the variations of Indian curries tracing their roots back in history and cherishing our present celebrations. And through this contest and my picture uploads ,I m sure to contribute towards the rich food cultural history of India and spread the same.
author: Tushareats

title: File:Surnoli dosa- Bangalore home-04 pic.jpg
description:
Traditional sweet pancake breakfast  item in Konkani households ( Gaud Saraswat Brahmins).Surnoli is a breakfast dosa item either slightly sweet the yellow version or not sweet the white version prepared mostly in Konkani households ( GSB) .Two versions of Surnali’s are prepared ‘Godi surnali’ (sweet dosa) and ‘Cheppi surnali ‘(bland dosa) .For cheppi surnali ignore adding jaggery,rest everything is same...Best part is was I just love the sweet batter.Surnali is best relished with homemade butter or ghee..But  I like it relish on its own  with chutney or ghee as I dislike  butter in direct form.
                                               This is one of the softest dosa.Traditionally a piece of fresh turmeric is added while grinding for the flavour and colour but we may add powder also.More the coconut is added softer the surnali’s turn out.The recipe is common among all Konkana’s with slight variations.The dosa batter includes turmeric, little jaggery,poha,curd,dosa rice ,parboiled rice all ground to a fine batter and fermented overnight. I have shared the pic of the dosa made in the traditional iron tawa  in our houseas is most of the dosa made in the coastal areas of Karnataka.

title: File:Idli (5194454248).jpg
description:
At the store, idli rice is sold in both sacks and bulk.  The rice is used in a flour to make an eponymous cake.
 
From  Wikipedia : "Idli is a south Indian savory cake popular throughout India. The cakes are usually two to three inches in diameter and are made by steaming a batter consisting of fermented black lentils (de-husked) and rice. The fermentation process breaks down the starches so that they are more readily metabolized by the body. Most often eaten at breakfast or as a snack, idlis are usually served in pairs with chutney, sambar, or other accompaniments. Mixtures of crushed dry spices such as milagai podi are the preferred condiment for idlis eaten on the go."
author: Leslie Seaton  from Seattle, WA, USA

title: File:Idli Chutney-Mangalore-Karnataka-DSC001.jpg
description: Idli is a type of savoury rice cake, originating from the Indian subcontinent, popular as breakfast foods in Southern India and in Sri Lanka. The cakes are made by steaming a batter consisting of fermented black lentils (de-husked) and rice. The fermentation process breaks down the starches so that they are more readily metabolised by the body. It has several variations, including rava idli, which is made from semolina. Regional variants include sanna of Konkan.

description:
Kempu Aritha Idli and Kadamba Chutney (Red Rice Steamed Cakes and Kadamba Idli)
 Red Rice Idli is a traditional South Indian breakfast item. It is made by soaking a variety of red rice and urad dal (Vigna Mungo) in water, grinding both with water, and leaving the mixture for fermentation. Next, it is steamed in an steamer. Kadamba chutney is made using Byadgi chillies and  roasted lentils tempered with groundnut oil and spices.

description:
Kempu Aritha Idli and Kadamba Chutney (Red Rice Steamed Cakes and Kadamba Idli)
 Red Rice Idli is a traditional South Indian breakfast item. It is made by soaking a variety of red rice and urad dal (Vigna Mungo) in water, grinding both with water, and leaving the mixture for fermentation. Next, it is steamed in an steamer. Kadamba chutney is made using Byadgi chillies and  roasted lentils tempered with groundnut oil and spices.
 
This is a closeup picture and underwent minimal processing to increase the brightness and warmth.

description: Beef Vindaloo - Chilli Mama, Chadstone AUD6.80 small I had a hankering for spice, lots of spice, and I wanted it hot. The beef vindaloo at Chilli Mama was the answer. title: File:Butter Chicken, Beef Vindaloo Lunch Thali - Spice Kitchen AUD9.90 (3694113488).jpg
description: Previously known variously as Copper Chimney or Jom Makan, both serving Muslim Indian food popular in Malaysia and Singapore, the latest incarnation is as Spice Kitchen, serving mostly Northern Indian food. David and I decided to go for the AUD9.90 lunch thali with 2 meat curries, naan, rice, papadum, salad and raiti, except mine was missing the raita. The butter chicken wasn't bad, creamy with bits of cashew nut, but a bit underspiced. The beef vindaloo was spicy hot, but again, lacking in the other warming spices, and very over seasoned! They also had a AUD12.95 All-You-Can-Eat lunch and dinner buffet, with 1 meat curry, 1 veg curry, butter chicken and potato and capsicum curry today, seekh kebab of minced lamb, onion bhaji, rice, garlic naan, papadam, salad and raita. Basically, it was mostly like a lunch thali, except more of it! Could be worth a try if I was really hungry. Spice Kitchen (03) 9663 3006 157 Lonsdale St Melbourne VIC 3000
author: Alpha  from Melbourne, Australia

It's a pity that there was quite a lot of ghee in the biryani. The first few mouthfuls were very good, with the buttery richness of the ghee, but I could only finish half. The other half will probably become leftover lunch, with a good helping of vegies to cut through the ghee! :)

title: File:Lumpia (52408045114).jpg
description:
RCL Spectrum of the Seas 
  Lumpia are various types of spring rolls commonly found in the Philippines and Indonesia. 
  Lumpia are made of thin paper-like or crepe-like pastry skin called "lumpia wrapper" enveloping savory or sweet fillings. It is often served as an appetizer or snack, and might be served deep fried.
 
Lumpia are Filipino and Indonesian adaptations of the Fukienese (Hok-Kian)  and Teochew popiah, which was created during the 17th century in the former Spanish colonial era.

title: File:Mac MG 5939.jpg
description: Kare Kare is a type of Filipino stew with a rich and thick peanut sauce. It is a popular dish in the Philippines served during special occasions. The traditional recipe is composed of ox tail. There are instances wherein both ox tripe and tail are used. The vegetable components of the dish are string beans, eggplant, bok choy, and banana blossoms. Lightly browned toasted ground rice is used to thicken the sauce.

title: File:Filipino roasted pig at Toledo Public Market 38.jpg
description: Cebuano Lechon Baboy is the undisputed crown jewel of Toledo City Public Market. Unlike other varieties, it is slow-roasted over charcoal while heavily stuffed with local aromatics like lemongrass, garlic, and scallions, creating incredibly savory, self-basting meat that requires no dipping sauce. Chopped freshly on-site, each serving blends exceptionally tender, juicy meat with fragments of its signature amber, glass-crisp crackling. This iconic delicacy is a celebrated centerpiece of Filipino gatherings and daily market life, delivering an unmatched burst of rich flavor and texture in every single bite.
author: QueenCityCebu

title: File:Illuminated Lechon Stalls.jpg
description: Brightly illuminated under a series of connected green tents, a row of bustling food stalls comes alive during a vibrant evening night market. The prominent booth in the foreground showcases traditional Cebu lechon, featuring menu boards with meal packages, large cooking pots, and a golden-brown roasted pig ready for hungry customers. Overhead bulbs cast a warm glow across the counter, while outdoor blue plastic tables and other stalls stretch into the background. This lively scene perfectly captures the energetic and welcoming atmosphere of local Filipino street food culture and night market gatherings.

title: File:Lechon Baboy sa Sugbo Mercado.jpg
description: Lechon Baboy at Sugbo Mercado is one of the most popular dishes. It is a whole roasted pig, seasoned with special spices and cooked until the skin is crispy and the meat remains juicy. It is usually served sliced and paired with vinegar and chili dipping sauce or other condiments. Lechon Baboy at Sugbo Mercado is an iconic dish in Cebu, known for its rich flavor, tenderness, and crispy skin.
author: IndayLiburan

title: File:Lechon Baboy sa Sugbo Mercado 1.jpg
description:
Lechon Baboy sa Sugbo Mercado is one of the standout dishes at the market, showcasing the best of Cebu’s culinary heritage. This iconic Filipino dish features a whole roasted pig, seasoned with a special mix of spices and cooked over an open flame until the skin is crispy and the meat is tender and juicy. It is usually served in slices, often paired with a vinegar-based dipping sauce or spicy condiments.
Lechon Baboy at Sugbo Mercado is a must-try for food enthusiasts, especially those who want to experience the rich, savory flavors that make Cebu's lechon famous. It’s perfect for sharing with friends or family in the vibrant and festive atmosphere of the market.
author: IndayLiburan

Lechon Belly at Sugbo Mercado is popular for its flavor, affordability, and the crispy skin that stays crunchy even after serving.

Lechón kawali involves boiling the processed meat, and then frying the pieces of pork in a frying pan.

title: File:Pho ga (noodle soup with chicken), Hanoi (6945821707).jpg
description:
Phở   or   pho   is a Vietnamese noodle soup consisting of broth, rice noodles called bánh phở, a few herbs, and meat, primarily made with either beef or chicken.
    Phở   is a popular street food in Vietnam and the specialty of a number of restaurant chains around the world. Pho originated in the early 20th century in northern Vietnam, and was popularized throughout the rest of the world by refugees after the Vietnam War. 
 
The Hanoi and Saigon styles of   phở   differ by noodle width, sweetness of broth, and choice of herbs. A related noodle soup, bún bò Huế, is associated with Huế in central Vietnam. Source:   en.wikipedia.org

title: File:Plain rice with crisp beef lungs, sambal eggplant and curried potatoes - Minang Nasi Padang AUD6.50 (3158454967).jpg
description: Following a tip from Aunt Lee Geok, we visited this little Indonesian place for lunch. We wanted to try Warung Agus, but they were closed for the Christmas break until 12 Jan 2009. From the logo in the shopfront, it definitely looked the part of a Minangkabau-style eatery, most well known for Nasi Padang, plain rice served with a variety of dishes. At AUD6.50 for 3 dishes plus rice, it's a bargain. The food is quite good, not too much chillis and well-rounded spices. The selection was on the small side, 4 meat dishes, 4 vegetable dishes and sambal egg. Julia got the beef rendang, fried chicken wings with a dark soy sauce and beansprouts. I got the crisp beef lungs, sambal eggplant and curried potatoes. The rendang was very tender, literally falls apart, and well-spiced. I love offal and the crisp beef lungs definitely did it for me. With just a hint of the metalic-tang typical of offal, most of the bits were crisp, but several slices were still nice and spongey. Drizzled with a sweet caramel dark soy sauce spiked with chilli, it is very yum! They also have a decent teh tarik, a forthy tea, for AUD2.20. Just remember to ask for it "kurang manis" (less sugar) if, like us, you like it with only half a tonne of sugar. :) Minang Nasi Padang Pelham Place, Carlton Near the corner of Swanston Street. Photos: - Shopfront - Turmeric rice with beef rendang, fried chicken wings with a dark soy sauce and beansprouts - AUD6.50 plus AUD0.50 for turmeric rice - Plain rice with crisp beef lungs, sambal eggplant and curried potatoes - AUD6.50 - Teh Tarik - AUD2.20 - Counter
author: Alpha  from Melbourne, Australia

title: File:DFC 0330 Grilled meat skewers topped with sliced red onion chopped herbs and a sprinkle of seasoning served alongside fresh lettuce.jpg
description: This photo shows a close-up of what appears to be satay or meat skewers - a popular street food in many Southeast Asian countries. The skewers feature small pieces of grilled or marinated meat (likely chicken, beef, or pork) on wooden sticks. They're garnished with thinly sliced red onions, chopped green onions or scallions, and what looks like a sprinkle of ground peanuts or spice mixture on top. On the left side of the image, there's a bit of fresh green lettuce leaf, which is often served alongside these skewers as a garnish or wrap. The meat has a rich, glazed appearance suggesting it's been marinated in a savory sauce before cooking. This style of food is particularly common in cuisines from Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and other parts of Southeast Asia, often served with dipping sauces like peanut sauce.
author: PattayaPatrol

title: File:DFC 2193 Sticky char-grilled skewers of savory satay glazed in a rich peanut sauce resting on a banana leaf.jpg
description: This photo shows a delicious serving of satay, which consists of small pieces of marinated meat (likely chicken or pork) threaded onto thin wooden skewers. The satay is glistening with a rich, brown peanut-based sauce that's pooled on the banana leaf beneath it. Satay is a popular street food in many Southeast Asian countries, particularly Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. The meat appears to be grilled to perfection, with a caramelized exterior, and the generous amount of sauce adds moisture and flavor. The presentation on the green banana leaf is traditional in many Southeast Asian cuisines.
author: PattayaPatrol

title: File:DSCF1097 Golden grilled chicken satay skewers laid out on banana leaves ready to serve at a bustling street-food stall.jpg
description: This photo shows a display of chicken satay, a popular Southeast Asian street food. The skewered pieces of meat appear to be marinated in a yellow curry-like seasoning, likely containing turmeric which gives them that distinctive golden color. The satay skewers are arranged neatly on a banana leaf that sits on what looks like a metal serving tray, typical of street food vendors or market stalls. Chicken satay is commonly served with a peanut dipping sauce, though the sauce isn't visible in this image. This dish is particularly popular in countries like Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Singapore, and is a common sight at night markets and food stalls throughout the region.
author: PattayaPatrol

title: File:Beef Rendang with Nasi Kuning and Green Beans.jpg
description:
Beef Rendag 
  Make a boemboe/paste in the blender from:
1 red onion, chopped
4 cloves of garlic, chopped
5 red chilies (deseeded) chopped
1/2 t kurkuma
1 t laos (I didn't have this fresh)
4 roasted kemiri-nuts (candlenut)
5 cm ginger, chopped
2 stalks lemongrass, finely chopped
  Take 1 can of coconutmilk, add the boemboe/paste and add:
2 leaves salaam (indonesian bay leaf)
2 lime leaves
salt
(30 gr toasted coconutflakes if you like)
  Bring to the boil and add 500 gram lean beef. 
Depending on the meat you use, simmer until the meat is tender and the sauce is thick and sticky. (It took me 4 hours)
Add salt or sambal oelek if needed. 
 
Serve with nasi kuning and green beans.
author: FotoosVanRobin

title: File:Nasi Kuning Daun Pisang.jpg
description: Nasi kuning daun pisang khas Gorontalo yang enak, wangi dan gurih. Nasi cukup pulen, berwarna kuning terang dengan aroma harum rempah. Disajikan dengan alas daun pisang, Nasi kuning Gorontalo menambah selera untuk sarapan pagi. Bakwan goreng atau tahu goreng menjadi pilihan untuk menemani nasi kuning khas daun pisang ini ditambah dengan sambal rica yang khas dan pedas. (Lokasi: Kab. Bone Bolango - Gorontalo).
author: Supardisahabu

title: File:Nasi Kuning Daun Woka.jpg
description: Nasi Kuning Daun Woka merupakan makanan khas dari Kota Manado, Sulawesi Utara. Makanan yang terbuat dari beras dengan bumbu kunyit, santan, serta rempah-rempah itu, biasanya menjadi hidangan spesial dalam acara pesta atau syukuran. Nasi Kuning ini dilengkapi irisan ikan cakalang, daging sapi, sambal, dan bawang goreng. Juga dapat ditambahkan sebutir telur ayam. Wadah Nasi Kuning ini tidak memakai kertas atau daun pisang, melainkan daun woka atau lontar. Daun lontar ini akan semakin membuat Nasi Kuning  lezat dan gurih. (Lokasi: Manado, Sulawesi Utara)
author: Supardisahabu

title: File:Nasi Kuning Ibu Sulastri.jpg
description: Delicious and succulent Nasi Kuning Ibu Sulastri, yellow rice colored with turmeric, surrounded by teri kacang (anchovy with peanuts), empal gepuk (sweet fried beef), udang balado (shrimp in chilli), urab (vegetables in shredded coconut dressing), and sambal goreng kentang (spicy potato). Yellow rice is considered as celebrative Indonesian dish and often made as Tumpeng (cone shaped rice with assortment of Indonesian dishes). Jakarta, Indonesia.
author: Gunawan Kartapranata

title: File:Nasi Kuning Manado.jpg
description:
Nasi Kuning Manado terbuat dari nasi yang dimasak menggunakan serai, daun pandan, daun jeruk, lengkuas, santan, garam dan kunyit. Lauk pendamping nasi kuning bisa berupa talas atau ubi goreng kering, abon ikan cakalang yang dimasak dengan santan, bihun, bawang goreng, semur daging dan telur rebus. Bagi yang suka pedas, sambal pelengkapnya sangat mengigit !
Nasi ini biasa dibungkus dengan daun woka (lontar).
author: Tumanisme

title: File:Nasi Kuning Tawau.jpg
description: Nasi Kuning is an Indonesian dish but is famous in Tawau.  The original ones includes sambal fish, coconut, slices of cucumber and hardboiled egg.  The rice is cooked with turmeric hence the name and color of the rice.  Nasi Kuning is translated to Yellow Rice.
author: Maslight

title: File:Nasi Kuning Telur.jpg
description: Nasi Kuning Gorontalo, Nasinya kuning terang, semerbak gurih aromanya. Ditaburi abon tuna dan diberi telur ayam rebus. Nasi kuning di Gorontalo disajikan dengan beragam variasi, mulai dengan taburan abon ikan cakalang yang menggoda, potongan daging yang lezat, laksa basah yang memikat, serta sambal rica yang pedas. (Tempat : Nasi kuning di Kota Gorontalo).
author: Supardisahabu

title: File:Nasi Kuning dan Ungkep Ayam.jpg
description: Yellow rice is a typical Indonesian food. This food is made from rice which is cooked together with turmeric and coconut milk and spices. With the addition of spices and coconut milk, yellow rice has a more savory taste than white rice and several side dishes such as Ungkep Chicken are served for needs during traditional activities in Indonesia.
author: RahmadHimawan Photography

title: File:Nasi Kuning khas Manado.jpg
description:
Nasi kuning Manado adalah salah satu jenis variasi nasi berbumbu kunyit yang menggunakan ikan cakalang sebagai lauknya, dan juga daun woka atau daun lontar sebagai pembungkus nasi kuning ini yang menjadi salah satu ciri khas hidangan asal Manado.
Dibungkus membentuk lonjong, nasi kuning ditemani dengan telur rebus, irisan telur dadar, ikan cakalang asap pedas, dengan tambahan sambal. Di Manado, menu ini sangat populer sebagai menu sarapan atau sebagai hidangan yang dijajakan di malam hari. Lokasi pengambilan gambar: RM Warung Regal Kota Gorontalo

title: File:DFC 4620 Zesty Thai larb salad with fresh mint crunchy greens and sliced boiled egg - a flavorful bite from Pattaya.jpg
description: This photo shows a beautifully presented Thai salad served on a rectangular turquoise plate. The dish appears to be a traditional larb or spicy minced meat salad, topped with fresh mint leaves, red onions, and what looks like ground toasted rice. On one side of the plate are halved boiled eggs, adding protein and visual contrast to the dish. The other side features some fresh lettuce leaves and a small portion of shredded vegetables or coleslaw. The salad sits in a light sauce or dressing, likely containing fish sauce, lime juice, and chili. The dish is presented on what appears to be a wooden table, highlighting the vibrant colors and fresh ingredients of this typical Thai cuisine from the Pattaya City area. This style of salad is known for balancing spicy, sour, sweet, and savory flavors that are characteristic of Thai cooking.
author: PattayaPatrol

title: File:DSC 9985 A vibrant plate of spicy minced meat salad larb tossed with fresh herbs red onion chopped green beans and a sprig of mint on top.jpg
description: This appears to be Larb, a popular Southeast Asian minced meat salad that's particularly common in Laotian and Thai cuisine. The dish consists of finely minced meat mixed with fresh herbs (like mint, which is visible in the image), red onions (showing their purple color), and various aromatics. The meat appears to be cooked and crumbly in texture, and it's garnished with fresh green herbs and purple red onion slices. The dish typically includes a dressing made with lime juice, fish sauce, and chili, though these liquid elements aren't immediately visible in the photo. Larb is known for its combination of spicy, sour, and savory flavors, and is often served with sticky rice or as part of a larger meal. The fresh herbs and bright garnishes give the dish an appetizing, fresh appearance.
author: PattayaPatrol

title: File:Twin 5” 38 Mk38 gun mount from “ROCS Kai Yang” at the 823 Artillery Battle Memorial Park, Taichung, Taiwan. 07-03-2026 (55255713036).jpg
description:
This twin gun is from the Gearing-class destroyer “ROCS Kai Yang” [DDG-924] which was originally commissioned by the US Navy in October 1945 as the “USS Richard B Anderson” [DD-786]. She earned four battle stars during the Korean War and a further eleven for her service in the Vietnam War.
She was transferred to Taiwan in June 1977, originally as [DD-924] but became [DDG-924] after modernisation in the 1980s. She was finally retired in November 1999 and later sunk as an artificial reef, with one of her Mk 38 twin 5”/38-caliber mounts being preserved here.
823 Artillery Battle Memorial Park, Taichung, Taiwan.
 
7th March 2026
author: Alan Wilson  from Peterborough, Cambs, UK

title: File:Nasi Lemak Sambal Cumi in Indonesia 1.jpg
description: Nasi lemak (Malay fragrant coconut rice) served with sambal cumi (squid in chili sauce), sambal teri (sambal with anchovy), teri kacang (peanuts and salted ancovy), half boiled egg, and slices of cucumber. The rice is sprinkled with bawang goreng (fried shallot), served in a restaurant in Indonesia. Although this dish is popularly known as a national dish of Malaysia, it is also considered as a native dish in Riau Islands and Riau provinces in Indonesia, where it often served with spicy freshwater fish or seafoods (fish, shrimp or squid).

title: File:Nasi Lemak with Fried Chicken - Village Park Restaurant (4589845661).jpg
description: The fried chicken is famous at Village Park. It is crusted in various herbs and curry spices and then deep fried to give a crisp skin and moist insides. The pounded lemongrass gave it a nice zing. It's also huge! So don't come here on a full stomach :) The coconut rice was very good too, with the balance of coconut milk and pandan just right. Not too greasy either. Village Park Restaurant No.5, Jalan SS21/37, Damansara Utama, 47400 Petaling Jaya. Tel: 03 7710 7860 Reviews: - Village Park Restaurant @ Damansara Utama - KampungBoyCityGal, 8 Nov 2007 - Village Park Restaurant @ Uptown, Damansara Utama - Written on September 5, 2009 – 11:00 am | by saimatkong - Village Park Nasi Lemak @ Damansara Uptown, PJ - V Keong 2009

title: File:Nasi Lemak with Rendang Beef - Jom Makan (436322132).jpg
description: Nasi Lemak with Rendang Beef AUD7.90. AUD6.90 for 2 dishes from the bain marie with plain rice rice. Mostly spicy dishes. The beef rendang was quite authentic with bits of turmeric leaf, star anise and cloves, but I found it lacking in shredded coconut that usually adds that extra dimension to the dish. Unfortunately all this was brought down by way too much oil, and not just because it was accompanied by coconut rice. The coconut rice was fine, if a bit soggy. I think I'll stick to Changi Village Nasi Lemak. Jom Makan Malaysian Cuisine 159 Lonsdale St Melbourne 3000 (03) 9663 3006 Update 2007.05.08: Still no improvement with the Lamb Biryani with Okra and Chickpea curries. Jom Makan Copper Chimney shopfront

title: File:Kue Lapis.jpg
description: Kue lapis is a traditional Indonesian cake that can be purchased at various places throughout Indonesia. This cake is characterized by its different colors forming horizontal or vertical stripes. The taste of kue lapis is generally sweet. The main ingredients of kue lapis are tapioca flour, wheat flour, coconut milk, and a mixture of sugar and salt to create the right sweetness. Due to the ease and low cost of production, kue lapis is often used as a home business venture. The photo was taken in Gianyar, Bali.
